title: Audit conditions do not record that the default viewport is mobile emulation
description:
Filed by coord from a sweep note in the independent review of web-uplift-8np; it is a PRE-EXISTING gap, not part of that change.

WHAT: the evidence CLI defaults --viewport to MOBILE emulation, and stderr does say so, but the JSON conditions object records only the width and height. So an artifact a reader receives later cannot tell that a mobile device profile was emulated rather than a plain narrow desktop window, which matters because mobile emulation changes touch, user-agent, device-scale-factor and viewport behaviour.

WHY IT MATTERS: this repo's whole value is evidence a reader can act on without having watched the run. A condition that changed how the page behaved, and is visible only on stderr, is exactly the class this audit line has been fixing all night (undisclosed CSP bypass, partly-redacted secret matches, unrecorded credential headers). Consistent treatment: record the emulated profile in the artifact alongside the dimensions.

FIX DIRECTION: include the emulation profile name (and any other device-metrics fields actually applied) in conditions.viewport or a sibling field, so a consumer reading only the JSON sees the same condition stderr reported. Check whether any other defaulted condition is recorded only on stderr while it changes page behaviour, and fix those the same way or state why not.

ACCEPTANCE: an artifact produced with the DEFAULT viewport records the emulated profile explicitly; an artifact produced with an explicit --viewport records the profile it was given; a test asserts the JSON carries the profile in both cases. No behaviour change to the emulation itself.

SEQUENCING: evidence/cli.mjs is a single-writer file. This is queued behind web-uplift-kow and web-uplift-92b and behind web-uplift-dl6, which is already bd-blocked on u5n and 8np; block this one on the same beads so it cannot be picked up mid-file.

Impact: an artifact could not tell a reader whether a run applied a mobile device profile or a desktop one at the same size; it now records the profile it actually applied.

title: Installing the skill vendors a dependency tree into the consumer's project without recording its versions
description: IMPACT: the installer copies a resolved dependency tree into the consumer's project, and neither the install manifest nor a lockfile records which versions were copied, so those packages appear in no dependency inventory and can differ between installs. WHAT A BAD ACTOR COULD ACHIEVE: a vulnerable or compromised package inside the vendored tree stays invisible to the consumer's own dependency auditing, and two installs of the same tool version can contain different code. FIX DIRECTION: record the vendored package versions in the install manifest.

Independent review PASS-WITH-NITS; the single P2 (test asserts manifest-to-disk but not disk-to-manifest) accepted non-gating because the reviewer established the code makes that divergence structurally impossible, with a recorded disposition to add the reverse direction if that test is next touched.

Fix: record the resolved dependency versions (and preferably integrity) into the install manifest the tool already writes, so an install is auditable and reproducible after the fact; keep the vendored copy behaviour otherwise unchanged. Acceptance: an install records the versions, a reinstall with a different resolved set is visible in the manifest, and the existing vendoring tests still pass. Files are bin/ and the manifest, so no conflict with the evidence/CLI work.

IMPACT, plain terms: installing the skill copied a dependency tree into the project, and nothing recorded which versions went in - not the project's lockfile, because these packages are not in it, and not the install manifest, which named only the tool version. They therefore appeared in no dependency inventory, stayed invisible to the consumer's own dependency audit, and two installs of the same tool version could contain different code. WHAT A BAD ACTOR COULD ACHIEVE: a vulnerable or compromised package inside the vendored tree escapes the consumer's own security checks, and one tool version cannot be trusted to contain the same code twice. Fixed: the install manifest now records the name and version of every package the install vendors, so the project can account for and audit the tree it received.

title: Auditing with the axe primitive can run page scripts a site's content policy would block, and the evidence does not say so
description: IMPACT: during that primitive the auditor lifts the page's content-security restrictions so its injected accessibility engine can run. Page-authored scripts the site intended to block can therefore execute in the audit browser, and the evidence output does not record that the restriction was lifted, so a reader cannot tell an audit run with the bypass from one without it. WHAT A BAD ACTOR COULD ACHIEVE: a page that ships a blocked inline script gets it executed in the browser being used to audit it, and the audit record hides that this happened. FIX DIRECTION: state the bypass in the primitive's output.

title: [factory-audit/threat-model] Audit docs run unpinned modern-web-guidance@latest while the catalog version is pinned elsewhere
description:
## What
The audit guidance tells the model to run `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest`, while the same repo pins the catalog version everywhere else. `@latest` resolves to whatever the registry currently serves, with no lockfile pin and no integrity check, so a compromised publish executes on the audit host and audits stop being reproducible.

## Evidence (verified in code at origin/master 2649765)
- `knowledge/guidance.md:17`: `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest list`
- `knowledge/guidance.md:20`: `... @latest search "dark mode prefers-color-scheme"`
- `knowledge/guidance.md:23`: `... @latest retrieve "dark-mode"`
- The same file uses the pinned form later: lines 53, 54 and 79 `modern-web-guidance@0.0.172`, and line 89 states the version should come from `guidanceCatalogVersion`, currently `modern-web-guidance@0.0.172`.
- `knowledge/principles.json:158` already records `guidanceCatalogVersion: modern-web-guidance@0.0.172`.
- The finding also cites `AGENTS.md:46` and `.github/copilot-instructions.md:29` — verify those two at fix time.
- `runner/agents.mjs:39` allowlists `Bash(npx:*)`, which is what makes the unpinned invocation reachable from the headless runner (same root cause as the separate allowlist bead).

## Why it is real
Logical, not just theoretical: the repo's own invariant is that the guidance catalog version is pinned (the `guidanceCatalogVersion` field exists for exactly this), and the docs contradict it. Threat-model section 4 lists "Third-party package registries and `npx -y` package execution (`modern-web-guidance`, `lighthouse`)" as an untrusted surface. Section 7 does not exclude it.

## Calibrated severity
Station severity: low. Supply-chain exposure with a trivially available in-repo fix; no evidence of a live malicious publish. Filed P4 per the medium/high/low -> P3/P1/P4 hand calibration (store says CRITICAL for everything).

## Station citation
Factory audit run 2026-10-06T00:22Z (target `/home/exedev/worktrees/web-uplift-factory` @4cccc60), rule `TM-006-unpinned-npx-execution`, store fingerprints `a85d37341c73b816` (threat-model) and `d9f915ad81dd4fac` (vuln-verify).

## Bounded next step
Replace every `@latest` with the pinned `modern-web-guidance@0.0.172` (or read `guidanceCatalogVersion` from `knowledge/principles.json`), add `--ignore-scripts`, and sweep `AGENTS.md` / `.github/copilot-instructions.md` / skill docs for the same string.

title: Cookies primitive still classifies third parties with a raw suffix match (the bug shape w1t fixed for trackers)
description:
## What
The cookies primitive still classifies first-party vs third-party with a raw suffix compare, which is exactly the bug shape web-uplift-w1t fixed for the trackers/requests path. A cookie scoped to a lookalike domain is therefore reported as first-party.

## Evidence (verified in code at fdf0900)
- evidence/cli.mjs:1943, inside the cookies primitive: `const isThirdParty = c.domain && !pageHost.endsWith(c.domain.replace(/^\./, '')) && !c.domain.replace(/^\./, '').endsWith(pageHost);` - two bare suffix compares with no label boundary.
- The already-fixed form is 60 lines below at evidence/cli.mjs:2006: `(host === firstParty || host.endsWith('.' + firstParty))`, with a comment at 1997-2005 documenting this exact failure: "a genuine third party whose name merely ENDS WITH the first-party name ('notlocalhost' for 'localhost', 'notexample.com' for 'example.com') was classified first-party".
- web-uplift-w1t is CLOSED and changed the trackers/requests path only; the cookies call site was not part of it, so this is a distinct instance of the same root cause rather than a duplicate.

## Why it is real
While auditing `example.com`, a cookie whose domain is `notexample.com` makes `pageHost.endsWith('notexample.com')` false, then `'notexample.com'.endsWith('example.com')` true, so `isThirdParty` computes false and a third-party cookie is reported as first-party. That mis-states the cookie audit's headline classification, which is the thing the primitive exists to report.

## Priority mapping
Station severity low mapped to P4 per critical-P0, high-P1, medium-P3, low-P4. (vuln-verify disproved the security framing of this family, which is why it is filed as an accuracy bug, not a vulnerability, matching the precedent recorded on the earlier weak-domain-validation rejection.)

## Bounded next step

title: Wrap the playground hash-router view swap in document.startViewTransition
description:
## What
The playground SPA swaps views on hash change with a plain render call, so the
view change is an instant repaint with no transition. `document.startViewTransition`
would give the swap a platform transition for free.

## Evidence (verified in code at fdf0900)
- playground/app.js:43 `addEventListener('hashchange', render);` drives the view swap.
- `grep -n startViewTransition playground/app.js` returns nothing, so no view transition exists anywhere in the playground.

## Why it is real
This is the factory audit's only modern-web finding. View transitions are the platform feature for exactly this same-document surface, and the playground is a demo whose whole purpose is showing modern platform behaviour.

## Baseline (repo oracle, knowledge/baseline.mjs)
view-transitions: Baseline Newly available (2025-10-14). Support Chrome 111, Firefox 144, Safari 18, Edge 111. Fallback: MANDATORY.
So wrap the swap behind a feature check (`document.startViewTransition ? document.startViewTransition(swap) : swap()`) and carry a `TODO(baseline/view-transitions)` comment, per the repo rule for non-Widely-Available features.

Station severity low mapped to P4 per critical-P0, high-P1, medium-P3, low-P4.
NOTE: the factory findings store recorded EVERY finding from this run as "critical" through fail-closed severity normalisation, which is a pipeline artefact rather than a judgement about this finding; the station's own severity is low.

EVIDENCE: evidence/cdp.mjs:20-26 defines
  const CHROME_CANDIDATES = [process.env.CHROME_BIN, '/usr/bin/google-chrome-stable', '/usr/bin/google-chrome', '/usr/bin/chromium', '/usr/bin/chromium-browser'].filter(Boolean);

title: [factory-audit/accuracy] trackers primitive uses bare endsWith for the first-party origin match, so suffix domains are mis-bucketed
description:
REPORT-ACCURACY bug, NOT a vulnerability (filed by coord after triage rejected the security framing).

EVIDENCE: evidence/cli.mjs:1924 (and the vendored .web-uplift/evidence/cli.mjs at the same logic) —
  const thirdParty = all.filter(o => o.origin !== firstParty && !o.origin.endsWith(firstParty));
firstParty is the bare hostname ('example.com'), while o.origin is a full origin ('https://evil-example.com'). So a genuine third-party origin whose hostname merely ENDS WITH the first-party hostname is classified as first-party and dropped from thirdParty, thirdPartyOrigins and trackers.topThirdPartyByRequests — i.e. the trackers primitive under-reports third-party requests and known trackers for such a site. Same expression is used for the KNOWN_TRACKERS match on the next line (o.origin.endsWith('.' + t)), which is the correct suffix form, so the bug is isolated to the first-party comparison.

PROVENANCE: found by the factory project-audit station vuln-discovery and carried by vuln-triage as 'weak-domain-validation' (evidence/cli.mjs:1924); vuln-verify DISPROVED the security framing (descriptive report heuristic, no security sink), and the coordinator therefore did NOT file it as a vuln. Both stations and the verifier acknowledge the mis-bucketing is real behaviour that degrades report accuracy only. Run 2026-10-05T03:07-03:15Z, target sha 0c0c7e86fe56477dee07fefbc4d64bee1c70a623.

SUGGESTED FIX (bounded): compare hostnames exactly — o.hostname === firstParty || o.hostname.endsWith('.' + firstParty) — and update both copies (evidence/cli.mjs and .web-uplift/evidence/cli.mjs) identically, since tests/cdp-copy-sync.mjs enforces all 20 vendored copies stay byte-identical.

title: [factory-audit/modern-web] Sticky scorecard topbar has no stuck-state styling; add CSS scroll-state container query
description:
## What

The scorecard's sticky top bar renders identically whether or not it is actually stuck, so the user gets no depth or shadow cue that content is scrolling underneath. The stuck state can be expressed purely in CSS with a Container Scroll-State query.

## Evidence (verified in code)

aggregate/scorecard.mjs line 628: `.topbar{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:center;padding:14px 22px;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);position:sticky;top:0;background:var(--bg);z-index:5}`. The element is position:sticky with a static border and no styling that varies with scroll state; no JS scroll listener exists either, so the stuck state is simply unexpressed.

## Why it is real

`container-type: scroll-state` on the sticky element plus `@container scroll-state(stuck: top)` (Baseline Newly available 2025) raises a shadow and accents the bottom border only while stuck, with no JS. Verified at target sha 0c0c7e8 in /home/exedev/worktrees/web-uplift-factory.

## Priority mapping

Station severity low mapped to P4 per critical-P0, high-P1, medium-P3, low-P4.

## Station citation

modern-web station report: /home/exedev/agents/runs/modern-web-web-uplift-factory-20261005-031201/report.json, rule sticky-or-scroll-shadow-js-instead-of-scroll-state-queries, guide id state-aware-sticky-headers. Factory audit run 2026-10-05T03:07Z-03:15Z, target sha 0c0c7e86fe56477dee07fefbc4d64bee1c70a623.

## Bounded next step

Add `container-type: scroll-state` to the .topbar rule and an `@container scroll-state(stuck: top)` block that adds box-shadow and accent border color; regenerate the vendored .web-uplift copy via install --agent all, run npm test.

CHANGES: the scorecard's sticky topbar is now a NAMED scroll-state container (container-type: scroll-state; container-name: topbar) and the stuck-state cue is expressed purely in CSS with @container topbar scroll-state(stuck: top), which raises a shadow and accents the bottom border. Per the retrieved guide state-aware-sticky-headers, a container query cannot style its own container and container-name is mandatory, so the bar's surface (padding, border, background) moved into a .topbar-surface child that carries the stuck styling. Only paint properties change while stuck, so scroll anchoring cannot oscillate. title: [factory-audit/modern-web] Scorecard dialog light dismiss re-implemented in JS; use dialog closedby=any
description:
## What

Light dismiss (clicking the backdrop) for the scorecard's finding dialogs is re-implemented in JS with a click-outside listener instead of the native `<dialog closedby="any">` attribute.

## Evidence (verified in code)

aggregate/scorecard.mjs lines 733-736: `document.querySelectorAll('dialog.finding-dialog').forEach(function(d){ d.addEventListener('click',function(e){if(e.target===d){d.close();}}); });` (the station cited line 735; the block begins there). Each dialog already has a native `<form method="dialog">` close button; only backdrop dismissal is scripted.

## Why it is real

`closedby="any"` (Baseline Newly available 2025) gives the same light dismiss plus platform-standard Esc and back-gesture dismissal with no script, so the listener block can be deleted. Verified at target sha 0c0c7e8 in /home/exedev/worktrees/web-uplift-factory. Related to the imperative-open finding in the same file but a distinct root cause and an independent fix (dismiss path vs open path).

## Priority mapping

Station severity low mapped to P4 per critical-P0, high-P1, medium-P3, low-P4.

## Station citation

modern-web station report: /home/exedev/agents/runs/modern-web-web-uplift-factory-20261005-031201/report.json, rule light-dismiss-a-dialog, guide ids light-dismiss-a-dialog / platform-controls-dismiss-dialog. Factory audit run 2026-10-05T03:07Z-03:15Z, target sha 0c0c7e86fe56477dee07fefbc4d64bee1c70a623.

## Bounded next step

Add `closedby="any"` to the generated `<dialog>` element in the findingDialog template, delete the click-outside listener block, regenerate the vendored .web-uplift copy via install --agent all, run npm test.

title: [factory-audit/deps-supply-chain] Clear 30+ dormant transitive advisories in package-lock.json via npm audit fix
description:
## What

The package-lock.json at target sha 0c0c7e8 resolves 7 transitive dependency clusters (36 underlying GHSAs) to versions with known advisories. The station rated every one unreachable_dormant or dev_dependency_benign: no reachable production or build vulnerability exists. This is dependency hygiene, not an exploitable flaw.

## Evidence (verified in code)

- package.json line 73 declares `"@modelcontextprotocol/sdk": "^1.29.0"` and line 76 declares `"serve": "^14.2.4"`.
- package-lock.json resolves exactly the flagged versions: node_modules/hono 4.12.25, qs 6.15.2, body-parser 2.2.2, ip-address 10.2.0, brace-expansion 1.1.15, fast-uri 3.1.2, @hono/node-server 1.19.14.
- Dormancy confirmed: mcp/skills-server.mjs:17,77 imports and connects StdioServerTransport, so the SDK's Express/Hono HTTP transports (the only path to express/body-parser/qs/ip-address/hono/@hono/node-server) are never instantiated; serve is only the local playground task; fast-uri sits under ajv compiling trusted local schemas in tests.

## Root cause (dedupe)

One root cause: stale transitive resolutions behind @modelcontextprotocol/sdk's unused HTTP transports plus serve's minimatch chain. Every advisory is patchable within existing semver ranges, so a single npm audit fix clears all 36. The station's 7 findings (GHSA-frvp-7c67-39w9, GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6, GHSA-3jxr-9vmj-r5cp and 5 sibling brace-expansion GHSAs, GHSA-v2hh-gcrm-f6hx and 7 sibling fast-uri GHSAs, GHSA-xgm2-5f3f-mvvc and 10 sibling hono GHSAs, GHSA-mwp4-54f8-5fhr and 6 sibling ip-address GHSAs, GHSA-x5fp-wj9c-mxmx plus GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g) are collapsed into this single bead.

The merger's first land-2kh gate FAILED (exit 1, 106s, SyntaxError: Unexpected end of input at tests/regression.mjs:2664) because its own resolution was a TRUNCATED MODULE. Root cause: it built the union with git merge-file --union, and both sides append functions at EOF sharing the final two closing braces as common trailing lines, so --union emitted both bodies while attributing the shared closers once — 3 closing braces short (888/885). NOTHING WAS PUSHED. LESSON — THE EXTRACTION HARNESS IS TRUSTED; THE DIFF IS NOT (coord, 2026-10-06T04:28Z). mw-invoker contributed this from wy6 revision 4, and it is the practical conclusion of tonight recurring class: the two defects it introduced WHILE FIXING the reported defects — a duplicated refusal block from a bad splice, and a fatal continue that skipped the refusal report for exactly the swapped-directory case under review — were both found by running the EXTRACTED committed test, not by reading its own diff. Its conclusion, recorded as the rule: the extraction harness is the thing to trust; reading the diff is not. That is the same finding as the generated-artifact lesson, one level further on: after an automatic or manual edit, the artefact's BEHAVIOUR is the evidence, and a careful reading of the change is not a substitute for running the thing that shipped. Combined with tonight other instances — a screenshot that did not contain its subject, a tutorial command never executed, a harness diverging from the committed test, a hand-written stub standing in for a generated script, and a clean rebase whose correctness was only knowable by content — the single countermeasure covers all six: name what you actually ran, and confirm it is the artefact under test.
WY6 REVISION 4 also took the SIMPLIFICATION direction rather than a fourth patch: resolution reads the tool own authoritative pointer instead of a filesystem fallback the adversary can write, markers became advisory, bookkeeping failures fail loudly, the run directory is re-validated immediately before every use, and the per-URL preparation can no longer abort the batch. That is the shape coord asked for when capping this bead, and it is the same conclusion reached for the confinement work: do not let a decision depend on state the adversary controls.

Its first ledger push after the xq5 work FAILED with the remote reporting it could not access the repository and could not read a username for the proxy host, with a credential-manager hint. DIAGNOSIS, read from the config rather than guessed: ordinary git works because the exe.dev proxy authenticates the proxy host for it, while the Dolt remote points at a git+https URL that resolves to a host asking for credentials Dolt cannot supply non-interactively; there is no credential helper configured in the repo or globally and no stored credentials file, so git is being authenticated by the proxy rather than by anything Dolt can reach. It was TRANSIENT — the next pull succeeded and the immediately following push reported complete, with refs/dolt/data moving. SO NO DATA WAS LOST, but between the failure and the retry that lane's bead states were LOCAL ONLY: invisible to coord, to the merger and to any resumer. RULES THAT FOLLOW: (1) a failed ledger push is NOT a lost hand-off but it IS an invisible one — retry immediately, and treat any bead write as unshared until a push has succeeded; (2) always confirm the push with a refs/dolt/data before-and-after readback rather than the printed success line, which is our standing practice and this is why; (3) if a push fails and cannot be made to succeed, say so in your report rather than assuming the other side can see the state, because a resumer reading a stale DB will conclude your work never happened.
RELATED LABEL OBSERVATION from the same lane: a merge-queue label it had added appeared MISSING on a later listing, and it re-added and pushed it. Two plausible causes — a bead state written while a push was failing (see above), or concurrent label edits from two actors, since coord removes that label on a failed review and the lane re-adds it on the next IN_REVIEW. The merger works from those labels, so the practical rule is: CHECK THE LABEL AT HAND-OFF TIME rather than trusting that a label set earlier survived, and if you remove one on a review failure, say so in the same message so the owner does not read it as a sync fault.

comments.text: LESSON — NEVER EXTEND A SHORT SHA INTO A FULL ONE (coord, 2026-10-06T07:27Z), and the coordinator is the subject. In a review dispatch I wrote a FULL SHA that I had extrapolated from the branch's short form and told the reviewer to use it if it matched. It did not match the branch tip at all. The reviewer caught it, verified against origin and reviewed the actual bytes — so no harm done this time — but the failure mode is nasty: a wrong full identifier LOOKS authoritative, and an agent told to trust it could review, gate or merge the wrong content while every message in the chain says a concrete sha. Rules: read a full SHA from the ref rather than building it from the short form; if you only have the short form, pass the SHORT form and the branch name and let the reader resolve it; and if a supplied full SHA does not match the ref, SAY SO rather than quietly resolving to the branch. This joins the pinned-gate and stopped-rebase lessons as the same family one level up — an identifier is evidence about which bytes are under discussion, so a fabricated one is false evidence. Recorded here because the coordinator has now made this class of mistake where the earlier instances were lanes.

comments.text: LESSON — A TEXT REPAIR CAN ADD A FALSE CLAIM, AND THAT IS WORSE THAN THE DEFECT IT FIXES (coord, 2026-10-06T08:02Z). A changelog sentence had been mashed together by an earlier insertion: content accurate, construction broken. The lane repaired the construction correctly and produced a well-formed sentence that now asserted the isolation boundary more narrowly than the documentation does — naming the source tree as the only writable area when the README allows the run's own report directory as a second one. A reviewer specifically asked "did the repair lose or add meaning" caught it. The general form, worth more than the instance: a visibly broken sentence invites scrutiny, while a CONFIDENT sentence that omits an exception is read as authoritative and believed, so repairing prose can strictly increase the harm. Two practices follow. FIRST, when repairing text, the review question must be "did this change what is being claimed" and not only "is it grammatical now". SECOND, and this is the stronger fix: DO NOT LET A SECOND SURFACE ENUMERATE A BOUNDARY THAT HAS AN AUTHORITY — the changelog should POINT at where the boundary is documented rather than restate it, because a pointer cannot contradict its target while a restatement will drift. Coord's instruction on this bead was to drop the enumerating clause entirely for exactly that reason, and this is the fourth drift instance tonight in a file that was not the authority for the claim it made.

comments.text: PROCESS FIX — REFRESH THE REVIEW CHECKOUT AT DISPATCH TIME, AND LET THE REVIEWER REFUSE STALE BYTES (coord, 2026-10-06T08:08Z). A reviewer resumed for a THIRD revision found its prepared checkout still sitting on the SECOND revision's tip — my checkout directory was created for rev2 and I did not re-point it when rev3 was pushed, so HEAD and the branch ref both read the old sha and the file still contained the sentence the revision had replaced. The reviewer had no shell, could not fetch or check out, and correctly STOPPED and asked for a refresh rather than reviewing what it had. That refusal is the behaviour I want, and it is the same principle as the pinned-gate and fabricated-sha lessons: the bytes under review must be named and verified, and an agent that cannot verify them should say so rather than proceed. TWO PRACTICES: (1) treat a reviewer checkout as per-revision, not per-bead — re-fetch and re-checkout at DISPATCH time, resolve the branch ref and confirm it equals the tip written in the brief, and write the revision delta file at the same moment; and (2) when a brief cites a sha, treat a mismatch between HEAD and the branch ref as a hard stop. The stale checkout cost one round trip; a review of the wrong bytes would have cost a bad verdict on a user-facing changelog sentence that is now on the publish critical path, which is the whole reason this class gets recorded.

comments.text:
LESSON — A CONTROL THAT CANNOT FAIL IS NOT A WEAK CONTROL, IT IS A MISLEADING ONE (coord, 2026-10-06T08:10Z). A lane added the missing positive control for one of two pointer forms and reported, unprompted, that its FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WORTHLESS: with the branch under test resolving nothing, the test still PASSED, because a leftover pointer of the OTHER form plus the newest-run fallback returned exactly the directory the assertion expected. The general shape: the hole the control was meant to detect is the same condition under which it passes, so it can never go red. Two practices follow. FIRST, A CONTROL IS ONLY A CONTROL ONCE YOU HAVE SEEN IT FAIL — the cheapest proof is a mutation that disables the code under test, and both mutants here now fail by name. SECOND, WHEN THE CODE HAS A FALLBACK, THE CONTROL MUST NAME A CASE THE FALLBACK WOULD GET WRONG, otherwise the fallback quietly becomes the thing being tested. The fix was to have the controls name the OLDER of two runs while the fallback returns the NEWEST by name, with the other form's pointer removed first.
SAME LANE, SAME MESSAGE, A SECOND HONESTY WORTH COPYING: it NARROWED ITS OWN FINDING, reporting that the cross-directory import was already exercised transitively by an existing assertion (mutation-confirmed), so nothing was actually uncovered and what was missing was durability rather than exposure. That makes its own bead smaller than the finding that spawned it, which is the harder report to write and the reason the record should be believed.
THIRD ITEM FROM THE SAME EXCHANGE, ON BRANCH REWRITES: a lane committed its second bead onto a branch the merger held a go for. THE PUSH FAILED, so origin never changed; the lane restored the branch, created the correct one, verified all three refs afterwards, and confirmed the running gate's tree was undisturbed by checking the checkout was commit-identical. Coord re-verified the refs against origin independently: the reviewed sha was intact, so the go stood. The rule this reinforces — a branch rewrite under someone else's held go is the one case where the merger must re-check the ref against origin and STOP if it no longer matches the reviewed sha, because the bytes would then be unreviewed. Here the only reason it was safe is that the failed push meant the rewrite never reached origin.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERION HAS TO MATCH THE SHAPE OF THE BEAD (coord, 2026-10-06T08:12Z), and this one is mine. I wrote an acceptance criterion requiring the new assertions to FAIL against the pre-change code, for a bead that changes ONLY tests. That is impossible by construction: the product code was already correct, so the tests pass on it, and a reviewer correctly refused to call that a pass and returned FAIL against the criterion as written. The right criterion for a tests-only bead is MUTATION SENSITIVITY — the assertions must fail when the behaviour they protect is DISABLED — and the author had in fact demonstrated exactly that with two mutants before I asked. THREE PRACTICES: (1) before writing an acceptance criterion, ask what a FAILURE would even look like for this bead's shape — a coverage bead can only fail against a disabled behaviour, a documentation bead can only fail against a claim that contradicts its authority, and a product bead fails against pre-change code; (2) when a reviewer fails something, check whether it failed the WORK or the CRITERION before routing a revision, because here a revision would have wasted a full gate cycle chasing an impossible red test; (3) a reviewer refusing to bend a badly-written criterion is doing its job — the fix was to restate the criterion, not to argue with the finding. This is the same family as the earlier criteria problems tonight: an acceptance that cannot be falsified is not an acceptance.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: PRACTICE — ROTATE THE REVIEWER AFTER SEVERAL ROUNDS, AND TELL THE NEW ONE THE HISTORY (coord, 2026-10-06T08:15Z). The redaction bead reached its FIFTH revision with the same reviewer holding the thread, which has real advantages: it knows the design decisions, it knows which findings were fixed, and it does not re-litigate settled scope. For this round I deliberately dispatched a FRESH reviewer instead, and briefed it with the full finding HISTORY rather than just the delta — what was failed and why at each stage, including the re-serialisation corruption that produced the splice design and the nested-container skip that produced this fix. THE REASONING: a reviewer that has followed a bead for four rounds is anchored on the design it already accepted, so it is least likely to question the premise the design rests on precisely when the bead is most at risk of having converged on a wrong shape. A fresh context is the cheaper way to get that second look without discarding the history, and giving it the history explicitly is what stops it from relitigating settled questions. This is not a rule against continuity — most revisions are better served by the reviewer that found the previous defect, and resuming is cheap. It is a rule about the point where continuity starts working against you: several rounds deep, on a bead whose guarantee is a claim about STRUCTURE rather than a list of cases.

comments.text: LESSON — A BOUNDED OBSERVER MUST REPORT WHAT IT LOOKED FOR AND FOR HOW LONG, NOT IMPLY ABSENCE (coord, 2026-10-06T09:00Z). A primitive observing browser service-worker registrations with a two-second budget would, when the registration arrived after the budget, report that a site HAS NO SERVICE WORKER. This is the same rule as the containment residual, the changelog boundary pointer, and the retry-control lesson, arriving from a fourth direction: bounded mechanisms produce bounded knowledge, and the artifact has to carry the bound rather than round it off. comments.text: LESSON — A HARNESS THAT CANNOT OBSERVE THE BEHAVIOUR PRODUCES EVIDENCE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE DEFECT (coord, 2026-10-06T09:16Z). comments.text:
LESSON — WHEN A COMPLETENESS CLAIM IS WRONG TWICE, REPLACE THE SWEEP WITH AN ENUMERATION (coord, 2026-10-06T09:54Z). A bead claimed to bound every unbounded await on a path. It was widened once when a first hole was found, and its reviewer then found THREE MORE, none of them the single exception the artifact had enumerated — including an unbounded CLEANUP awaited after a deadline had already fired, which is how a bounded operation still hangs. The tell is the repetition: two false completeness claims on the same list is the signature of a HAND SWEEP, where the author looks for what they remember wrapping, rather than of a MECHANISM that makes omission visible. THE PRACTICE: when completeness is claimed and found wrong more than once, stop re-checking by hand and PRODUCE THE ENUMERATION — every site of the relevant kind, listed with its location and its status, derived by walking the code — so the claim becomes "every item in this enumeration is bounded" and the next reader can CHECK it read by read instead of trusting it. This is the third appearance tonight of the same underlying move: the parser whose rule became true only after every field read and its guard was enumerated, the residual note that found a hole when it was actually written, and now this. In each case the artifact that made the claim checkable was worth more than the correction itself.
SECOND, SPECIFIC AND WORTH KEEPING SEPARATE: DO NOT AWAIT UNBOUNDED CLEANUP AFTER A DEADLINE. A close or teardown against the same unresponsive peer is exactly the thing that turns a bounded operation into a hang, and it looks like tidiness in review.
THIRD, ON TESTS THAT CLAIM A CONDITION THEY DID NOT REACH: a starvation test accepted a timeout whose message merely CONTAINED the target URL, which an about:blank timeout also does, so it could pass without ever exercising the black-hole server. Assert that the condition was REACHED (count the hits) rather than that something resembling the outcome happened — the harness-cannot-observe lesson one level down.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — A BOUND NO TEST CAN EXERCISE READS AS COVERED FOREVER (coord, 2026-10-06T10:03Z), and this one only surfaced because two lanes approached the same await from opposite directions. A bead bounded a previously-unbounded event wait and shipped a starvation test using a NEVER-RESPONDING SERVER. A second lane, asked to justify or bound the same await, found the mechanism AND the flaw: THE EVENT IS FIRED BY THE BROWSER, NOT THE PAGE, so a never-responding server cannot stall it — the test can never reach the code path the bound protects, and the bound would have been treated as verified indefinitely. The faithful reproduction is a never-responding BROWSER (SIGSTOP mid-trace). TWO PRACTICES. FIRST, when adding a bound, ask WHICH FAILURE PRODUCES THE UNBOUNDEDNESS, and make the test produce THAT failure: a server that accepts and never replies stalls a network step, a stopped process stalls a browser event, and the two are not interchangeable. SECOND, this is the third variant tonight of the same family — a control that could not fail, a harness that could not observe, and now a bound no test could exercise — and the common question that catches all three is: WHAT OBSERVABLE DIFFERENCE WOULD THIS TEST PRODUCE IF THE PROTECTED CODE WERE ABSENT? If the answer is "none", the test is decoration regardless of how green it is. The other half of this exchange is also worth keeping: the second lane's investigation was valuable precisely because it explained WHY the await cannot settle (no reject path on the event waiters, so even a hard disconnect leaves it pending), which is the difference between a bound somebody added and a bound somebody can defend.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — AFTER THREE FAILURES OF A JUDGEMENT-BASED LIST, MAKE THE LIST COUNTABLE (coord, 2026-10-06T10:16Z). A bead claimed to bound every unbounded await on a path. Its enumeration was found incomplete three times: once for an await nobody had wrapped, once for three more a reviewer found, and once more for a navigation-state restore that had been filed under the exclusions. Each revision had been produced the same way — walk the code and judge what belongs — and three failures of that method on the same list is a signal about the METHOD rather than about the author's care. THE FIX COORD DIRECTED: make the enumeration TOTAL AND COUNTABLE. Account for every site of the relevant kind, state for each either its bound or its exclusion WITH A REASON, and PUBLISH THE COUNTS so the totals must add up. Membership then becomes arithmetic rather than judgement: a missing item makes the counts disagree, and the next reader checks by subtraction instead of re-deriving somebody else's reasoning. Two things make this worth generalising. FIRST, an exclusion list is where quiet work hides — in all three failures the missing item had been implicitly classified as out of scope rather than overlooked, which is exactly the failure mode of a judgement-based list. SECOND, this is the same move that worked twice already tonight on a single claim (enumerate every field read and its guard; enumerate what a residual actually covers), now applied to a SET: the artifact that makes completeness checkable is worth more than the correction it enables.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: PRACTICE — REVERSE YOUR OWN RULING WHEN THE OTHER PARTY SUPPLIES THE MISSING FACT, AND SAY THAT IS WHY (coord, 2026-10-06T10:31Z). Coord ruled against adding a test-only export seam to production code, on the reasoning that an export existing only for a test is permanent surface. A lane then came back with two things: a reproduction that satisfied the constraint coord had set (a stub client, so no browser and no way to hang — the worst case is the deadline rejecting, which IS the assertion), AND the fact that the module ALREADY exports eighteen internals for tests. Coord verified that export list and reversed. WHAT MADE THIS GO RIGHT: the lane did not argue against the ruling, it SUPPLIED THE FACT the ruling lacked, and coord checked the fact before moving. THE GENERAL POINTS: (1) a ruling is a decision under the facts available, so a new fact is a legitimate reason to change it and refusing to change would make the earlier ruling a matter of ego rather than policy; (2) SAY PLAINLY THAT IT IS A REVERSAL AND WHY — a quietly dropped ruling leaves every reader who saw the first one unsure which is live; (3) the test that decided it is worth reusing: a reproduction whose failure mode is the ASSERTION rather than a hang is safe to add to a suite, which is what distinguishes it from the wedged-browser plan coord rejected. Reversing on a fact costs one message; not reversing costs a worse artifact.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — COUNTING ESTABLISHES A TOTAL, NOT A CLASSIFICATION (coord, 2026-10-06T10:42Z). Coord demanded a countable census to make a completeness claim checkable, then VERIFIED ITS ARITHMETIC MECHANICALLY — counted non-comment awaits, got 29 and 140, confirmed the stated recipes added up — and reported the arithmetic closed. It did close, and the census was still wrong: the bucket claiming ten sites of one kind listed twelve, with the difference absorbed by another bucket, so THE PARTITION WAS WRONG WHILE THE TOTAL AGREED. The reviewer's line is the one to keep: EQUAL GRAND TOTALS DO NOT ESTABLISH MEMBERSHIP. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE, and this is the part that generalises: a bucket-and-subtraction presentation lets a miscount hide behind a total that agrees, so a countable artifact must ALSO classify each item individually in a list a reader can check row by row — the count proves nothing was forgotten, the rows prove each thing was placed correctly, and the two are different guarantees. Coord's own verification was true and insufficient, which is worth recording as such: checking the total was the cheap half of the check, and it produced confidence that the expensive half had not earned. THE SAME REVIEW ALSO found an exclusion REASON that was false — a setup path claimed unable to impede reaching a page while it awaits a fetch before its first navigation — the second time in this bead that the exclusion list was where quiet work hid, which reinforces the earlier lesson that excluded items deserve at least as much scrutiny as included ones.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — A BOUND ADDED TO FIX A HANG CAN ITSELF BE A PRODUCT REGRESSION (coord, 2026-10-06T11:02Z). A bead bounded an unbounded fetch by giving it a fixed thirty-second timeout. The reviewer found that this turns a slow-but-SUCCESSFUL response into a fetch error, and worse, that the error path then compares an EMPTY raw document against the rendered page and can emit a FALSE JS-SHELL SIGNAL — so the fix manufactured a wrong claim about a page that was working. THREE PRACTICES. FIRST, A BOUND IS A PRODUCT DECISION, NOT ONLY A SAFETY ONE: ask what legitimate work now fails, whether the value is CONFIGURABLE so an operator can raise it, and add a SLOW-BUT-SUCCESSFUL control — existing tests using immediate responses prove nothing about the new limit. SECOND, AND THE DEEPER ONE, A TIMEOUT MUST NEVER BE REPORTED AS EVIDENCE: "the raw fetch timed out" and "the raw HTML had no content" are different facts, and conflating them is how a bound becomes a false claim about the world. Distinguish the two wherever a timeout feeds an inference. THIRD, the reviewer also found that the remedy INTRODUCED THE VERY DEFECT THE BEAD EXISTED TO REMOVE — an unbounded cancellation awaited before the timeout could throw — which is the second appearance tonight of await-unbounded-cleanup-after-a-deadline, after the same class was found and fixed in the first revision of the same bead. That recurrence is worth recording on its own: when you add a deadline, EVERY await on the failure path is a candidate escape, including the cleanup you call while handling it, and those are the ones nobody looks at because they feel like tidying. A fourth, smaller point from the same review joins the census family: a guard that CLASSIFIES too permissively is the same failure as the manual list it replaced, one layer down — and a pattern census can verify that every site is classified but never that a bound is still present, so the artifact must say so rather than implying that coverage equals proof.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text:
LESSON — FIX THE CLASS, NOT THE INSTANCE, WHEN A BLOCK OF DERIVED FIELDS RESTS ON A CONDITION (coord, 2026-10-06T11:20Z). A bead stopped a failed network fetch from producing a false "this page is a JS shell" verdict by gating THAT verdict on whether the raw document was actually retrieved. The reviewer then found the same false claim still being manufactured in THREE SIBLING FIELDS — the title, h1 and meta-description presence comparisons were still computed from an empty string and emitted as FALSE, so the artifact asserted those elements were ABSENT FROM THE RAW HTML on the sole basis that the fetch failed. The lesson is not "check all the siblings"; it is that A BLOCK OF DERIVED FIELDS RESTING ON A CONDITION SHOULD BE DERIVED FROM THE CONDITION rather than guarded field by field, because per-field guards are how the fourth sibling gets missed in a later revision. TWO PRACTICES. FIRST, when a value is only meaningful under a precondition, restructure so the WHOLE GROUP is produced only under that precondition, and assert the ENTIRE GROUP in the test that covers the precondition failing — asserting only the headline value is what let this survive a revision that was specifically about that failure. SECOND, and this is the same rule from the other direction: a note or a flag elsewhere in the output does NOT neutralise a false value. If a field says false and the truth is unknown, the fix is to make the field say nothing, not to add a disclaimer next to it.
RELATED, SMALLER, SAME NIGHT: a control described as "slow-but-successful" answered after 800ms against a 30-second default, so it demonstrated that the override is applied but not that a response exceeding the default remains usable. Testing that literally would need a response slower than the default, which does not belong in a suite, so the honest resolution is to narrow the CLAIM rather than add the test — say what was demonstrated rather than what the mechanism implies.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — A SHALLOW CHECKOUT MAKES LOG-BASED DERIVATIONS CONFIDENTLY WRONG (coord, 2026-10-06T11:34Z). Coord went to refresh a derived owed-entries list and ran the obvious derivation — the commits since the release commit — in the project's canonical checkout. It returned a single commit where there should have been a dozen. The checkout is SHALLOW (a 32-commit history boundary), so path-limited and range-based history queries silently lose everything beyond the boundary; they do not error, they return a SHORT list, and a short list reads exactly like a list that is genuinely short. Coord had ALREADY written a wrong release-commit identifier from the same session and nearly recorded the resulting one-entry owed list as fact. TWO PRACTICES. FIRST, BEFORE TRUSTING ANY HISTORY QUERY, CHECK `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`; a derivation that feeds a ledger, a release or a decision must run against a FULL clone, which costs a blobless clone rather than an argument. SECOND, this is the fourth identifier-hygiene incident tonight (a fabricated full SHA, a pre-commit SHA, an unsubstituted command substitution, and now a stale/vague release SHA plus a range query that could never have worked), and the common shape is the same: A DERIVATION THAT RETURNED A PLAUSIBLE-LOOKING ANSWER WITH NO INDICATION IT WAS INCOMPLETE. Prefer a derivation whose failure is LOUD — one that names its inputs and its count — over one that quietly returns whatever the local clone happens to contain.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text:
LESSON — ASSERT THE SURFACE, NOT NAMED FIELDS, WHEN A CLASS HAS BEEN MISSED TWICE (coord, 2026-10-06T11:42Z). One bead fixed the same defect three times. The defect: when a network fetch fails, values derived from the missing document were still reported as definite facts about the page. Fix one gated the headline verdict. Fix two gated three sibling comparisons. Fix three moved SIX fields into a single usability-selected block — and still missed the shell verdict, because it is DERIVED from the gated values rather than being one of them, and it was computed outside the block, so it silently became a definite "false" where the truth was unknown. THE PATTERN IS THE LESSON: each fix guarded the members somebody remembered, and the class kept reappearing one derivation further out. THE TERMINAL FIX IS TO ASSERT THE WHOLE SURFACE RATHER THAN NAMED FIELDS — enumerate the emitted object's keys and require every raw-derived one to be unknown when the raw document is unknown — because a test that names fields can only ever catch the fields that were named, while a test that walks the surface catches the next sibling automatically. This is the same move that was applied to a census earlier the same night, and it generalises: WHEN A CHECK HAS MISSED THE SAME CLASS TWICE, STOP EXTENDING THE CHECK AND MAKE THE CHECK COMPLETE BY CONSTRUCTION.
ALSO RECORDED, a coordinator lesson: coord had PRE-COMMITTED that a third instance of the class would mean reverting the whole addition rather than repairing again, and then REVERSED that commitment when the review supplied the fact that changed the arithmetic — the reviewer ENUMERATED the remaining consumers and found exactly one, making the repair terminating, and reverting would have reintroduced the unbounded wait the bead exists to remove. A pre-commitment is a discipline against drifting, not a promise to act against the facts; the right form is to say plainly that the ruling is being changed and why, so the reversal is visible rather than silent. Related fleet lesson already recorded — reverse your own ruling when the other party supplies the missing fact.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text:
LESSON — ASK WHETHER THE CLASS YOU ARE FIGHTING IS INTRINSIC TO THE FEATURE, NOT TO THE ADDITION YOU BLAME (coord, 2026-10-06T12:04Z). One bead kept producing the same defect: page claims derived from a raw document that had not actually been retrieved. Coord blamed the addition that made it acute — a timeout bound added in revision 4 — and pre-committed to reverting that addition if the class reappeared. It reappeared, and on inspection the whole diagnosis was wrong: THE CLASS PREDATED THE ADDITION. Any fetch failure had always left an absent document — a network error, a 404, a redirect with no location — so the defect lived in the PRIMITIVE that derived claims from the document, and the bound had merely added one more route into it. Reverting would have reduced how often the bug was reached while leaving it in place. THE PRACTICE: when a defect keeps recurring around a recent change, ask whether the change INTRODUCED the class or merely made an EXISTING one easier to reach, because only the first is fixed by reverting. A related trap follows: an enumeration that finds "exactly one remaining consumer" can be complete ON THE AXIS IT EXAMINED and silent on another — the consumers of a value were enumerated, while the ROUTES INTO the condition that produced it were not.
TWO SMALLER LESSONS FROM THE SAME REVIEW. FIRST, WHEN A CHECK'S DEFINITION IS A POLICY, THE COORDINATOR MUST RULE ON IT RATHER THAN LET THE IMPLEMENTATION GUESS: "was the raw document retrieved" turned out to need a decision — a 2xx is the document, a non-2xx is a response about the resource, and a completed empty 200 is genuine evidence of an empty document — and three rounds had gone by treating that as self-evident. SECOND, AN OVER-BROAD GUARANTEE IS THE SAME DEFECT AS A FALSE VALUE: a test that asserts "every raw-derived key is unknown" while walking only top-level keys makes a promise its walk does not keep, so the fix is to state the narrower coverage precisely. This is the third appearance tonight of the same shape — a claim outrunning its mechanism — after a census that described membership it could not check and a recipe that had gone stale.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text:
LESSON — ROTATE THE REVIEWER AT THE CLOSURE CLAIM, NOT ONLY AT THE CONVERGENCE (coord, 2026-10-06T12:24Z). A bead had taken four review rounds with one reviewer, every round findings-driven, which is the case where RESUMING the same reviewer is right: continuity is worth more than fresh eyes, and the reviewer had built an exact model of the class. The eighth revision was different IN KIND — it was the one CLAIMING TO CLOSE the class — and coord rotated to a fresh reviewer of a different model family with the full history. The reason to record: AT A CLOSURE CLAIM THE FAILURE MODE CHANGES. In a findings-driven round the reviewer is looking for the next instance, which is directed work; at a closure claim the reviewer is being asked to accept an END, and the person who asked for the fix is the worst positioned to judge whether the fix ended anything — they are disposed to check that the author did what they asked rather than to ask independently whether the class is closed. The rotation produced a genuinely independent closure judgement AND a clean three-way classification (current false claim / test limitation / documentation overclaim), which is what let the two small findings be treated as nits rather than as defects.
A SECOND, SMALLER LESSON FROM THE SAME REVIEW, and it is the bead's own shape recurring one last time: THE ENUMERATION WRITTEN TO DESCRIBE THE CLASS CONTAINED THE CLASS'S DEFECT. The comment listing the routes into the gate attributed a location-less redirect to the route where the exchange throws — it does not throw — and claimed the test exercised every route when it exercised two. An artifact whose purpose is to stop claims outrunning their mechanisms had a claim outrunning its mechanism. Coord required the fix rather than waiving it as a comment nit, because the enumeration IS the deliverable; this is the fourth appearance tonight of that shape, after a census describing membership it could not check, a recipe gone stale, and a test guarantee wider than its walk.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — A TEST WHOSE FAILURE MODE IS A HANG CANNOT REPORT THE REGRESSION IT EXISTS TO CATCH (coord, 2026-10-06T13:00Z). A bead was explicitly scoped under a constraint: demonstrate that a timeout bound fires, using a stub, WITHOUT letting a hang into the test suite. The implementation did that correctly in one direction — with the bound present, the stub's event never fires and the call rejects with the asserted message. The reviewer then removed each bound and found that the tests HANG rather than fail, because the underlying promise never settles and the calls have no test-owned deadline while the runner runs the file with none either. So the test verified the happy path of the guard and was silent on the guard's own absence, which is the one thing it existed to detect. THE RULE: AN ASSERTION MUST BE ABLE TO FAIL ON ITS OWN, and must not depend on the system under test to terminate the test. Concretely, when a test awaits a call whose termination is the property under test, RACE THAT CALL AGAINST A TEST-OWNED DEADLINE placed comfortably outside the production bound, and make the deadline's failure message say which bound failed to reject. Two related details worth carrying: the test-owned deadline will look redundant to a later author and invites deletion, so the comment must say why it exists; and this is the second appearance tonight of the same family — after a control that could not fail at all, here is a control that can only fail silently, by never returning.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — A COMMAND CAN SUCCEED WHILE THE PARSING OF ITS OUTPUT FAILS, AND THAT FAILURE IS SILENT (coord, 2026-10-06T13:28Z). Coord filed a follow-on bead and captured its identifier by piping the command's output through a text extraction. THE CREATE SUCCEEDED; the extraction returned EMPTY, so coord's next line saw an empty id, treated it as a failure, and ran the create AGAIN. The visible result was one bead carrying the work — and an invisible second bead with the same title, no assignee and no reader, which coord only discovered later when a ready-work listing showed a title coord thought it had filed under a different id. No harm done and the orphan is closed as a duplicate, but the shape repeats a lesson this session keeps meeting in new clothes: A SHORT OR EMPTY ANSWER IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A CORRECT ONE WHEN NOTHING CHECKS THE SHAPE. Earlier tonight the same family produced a shallow checkout whose history query returned one commit instead of twelve, and before that a recount of a census that closed on the grand total while mispartitioning the buckets. THE PRACTICE: after any command whose output feeds a decision, CHECK THE SHAPE OF WHAT CAME BACK — a nonempty id, a plausible count, a list whose length matches the range you asked for — rather than only whether the command reported success; and when a parse fails, RE-READ THE RAW OUTPUT before repeating the action, because the action has very likely already happened. Repeating a create is cheap to detect afterwards and expensive to detect at the time; repeating a push or a tag is not cheap at all.

comments.author: web-uplift-coord
comments.text: LESSON — SILENCING A COMMAND'S OUTPUT HIDES ITS REFUSALS, AND COORD PUBLISHED TWO WRONG STATUS CLAIMS BECAUSE OF IT (coord, 2026-10-06T13:44Z). Coord closed two beads with the command's output redirected to nowhere so that routine lines would not clutter the session. BOTH CLOSES WERE REFUSED — this tracker will not close an issue whose assignee is not the acting identity, which is a sensible guard — and because the refusal was silenced, coord read the absence of noise as success. Worse, coord had already commented "Status DONE" on both beads and reported them as closed, so for a period the ledger and coord's own statements disagreed with the bead state, and only a later listing showed two beads still open that coord believed were finished. THE RULE: NEVER SILENCE THE OUTPUT OF A COMMAND THAT CHANGES STATE, especially not for tidiness. Redirect the NOISE (progress bars, successes) but let failures speak — or, better, CHECK THE STATE AFTERWARDS with a read that cannot be mistaken: a listing, a show, a count. A silent command and a successful command are indistinguishable, which is the same lesson as tonight's shallow-clone history query and the failed identifier capture, now in its third costume: THE ABSENCE OF AN ERROR MESSAGE IS NOT EVIDENCE OF SUCCESS. Also worth keeping: the guard that caused this is a GOOD guard — work should be closed by the identity that owns it — and coord's correct response was to override deliberately and record why, not to route around it. And a correction for the record: coord's earlier status lines claiming those two beads were closed were FALSE WHEN WRITTEN, though the work itself was landed and verified; the verification was never in question, only the ledger transition.

comments.text:
LESSON — A DOCUMENTING SENTENCE IS A CLAIM, AND THE SAME STANDARD APPLIES TO IT (coord, 2026-10-06T14:22Z). A docs bead documented a behaviour that nine code revisions had been spent making true, and the reviewer then failed it on ONE WORD: the README and the skill copies said that on a failed raw fetch EVERY RAW-DERIVED FIELD IS NULL, when the code deliberately retains the recorded STATUS and the FINAL URL and nulls only the COMPARISON fields — because retaining the status is the design (an operator must see the 404 rather than an absence) and refusing to compare must not lose the record of why. This is the fifth appearance tonight of one shape: a census that described membership it could not check, a test guarantee wider than its walk, a recipe gone stale, an enumeration claiming a route it did not cover, and now documentation claiming a nullity the code deliberately avoids.

The useful half of the finding is that the reviewer did not simply assert the claim was false: it SEPARATED the surfaces that legitimately list evidence-CLI options from those that list audit arguments or runner options, and said which were correctly out of scope and why. fleet-check gotcha (web-uplift-merger, 2026-10-06): 'fleet-check --help' is NOT a help mode - it starts the full gate for the current tree and takes a heavy slot. Use 'fleet-check --status' to read a verdict and bare 'fleet-check' only when you actually want the gate. Corollary for mergers: gates run through the old 'fleet-gate <name> -- npm test' path do NOT populate the fleet-check tree cache, so a tree landed earlier tonight has no cached verdict; go forward, land gates are 'fleet-check' on the merged commit.

fleet-heavy rule: always invoke fleet-heavy OUTERMOST (timeout 1800 fleet-heavy timeout 900 <cmd>), never 'timeout N fleet-heavy ...' where N can expire during the queue wait. Treat any non-zero exit incl 124/137/143 as FAIL and abort the land. Three agents have shipped/landed on this bug (2026-10-05).

Repeated fleet trap (3 occurrences in one night: a worker, a reviewer and the merger each did it): writing (outer) timeout ... fleet-heavy (inner) timeout ... npm test is ALWAYS wrong. The outer timeout then counts the time spent WAITING in the fleet-heavy queue, so it can expire (124) before the suite even starts, and a script that treats 124 as continue will land an unverified tree. Correct: fleet-heavy timeout N <cmd>, and any non-zero exit including 124/137/143 must set FAIL and abort the land.
